_comment: CELPIP Reading Part 3: Reading for Information. Four paragraphs (A-D); each statement matches one paragraph, or E if none. 'answer' is the index in the task's options (A=0 ... E=4).

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Community gardens have become a familiar sight in many Canadian cities. In a community garden, a piece of land is divided into small plots, and local residents rent a plot for the growing season, usually for a small yearly fee. Toronto alone has more than 80 community gardens, many of them on land owned by the city. Most gardens have long waiting lists, and in some neighbourhoods people wait three or four years before a plot becomes available.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The benefits go beyond fresh vegetables. Researchers have found that people with community plots report lower stress levels and spend more time outdoors than people without gardens. Community gardens also bring together neighbours who might otherwise never meet. Many gardens organize shared work days, seed exchanges and harvest dinners, and some donate part of their harvest to local food banks.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Starting a new garden is not always easy. Groups must find suitable land, which is difficult in crowded downtown areas, and the soil must be tested, since old industrial sites can contain harmful chemicals. Water is another challenge: gardens need a reliable water supply, and installing pipes can cost thousands of dollars. Some cities now offer small grants to help new garden groups with these costs.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: To make the most of limited space, some gardeners are moving up. Rooftop gardens on schools, hospitals and apartment buildings are becoming more common, and in one Montreal neighbourhood, a large rooftop farm supplies vegetables to nearby grocery stores. Other groups use raised beds, which are easier for older gardeners and people in wheelchairs to reach. These new designs allow more people to garden, even where there is little open land.

tasks.intro: Decide which paragraph, A to D, contains each piece of information. If none of the paragraphs contains it, choose E.

option_labels.E: Not given in any of the paragraphs

questions.explanation: No paragraph gives this information.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: About one in eight Canadian workers works outside regular daytime hours. Nurses, factory workers, truck drivers and security guards are among the many people whose jobs require them to work through the night. As more businesses offer services twenty-four hours a day, the number of night-shift jobs has been growing, particularly in warehouses that ship online orders.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Working at night goes against the body's natural clock, which tells us to sleep when it is dark. Night-shift workers often sleep less than six hours during the day, because daylight, traffic and family activities make it hard to rest. Over time, this lack of sleep can affect mood and concentration. Some studies have also linked many years of night work to a higher risk of heart disease.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Experts recommend several ways to sleep better during the day. Blackout curtains keep the bedroom dark, and earplugs or a fan can block outside noise. Workers are advised to avoid caffeine in the last few hours of their shift and to keep the same sleep schedule on their days off, even though this can make it harder to spend time with friends and family.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Employers can also help. Some companies schedule shifts that rotate forward, from day to evening to night, which is easier for the body than rotating backward. Others provide quiet rooms where workers can take short naps during breaks. One Ontario hospital that introduced nap rooms for night nurses reported fewer mistakes and higher job satisfaction within a year.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Public libraries across Canada are lending far more than books. In some cities, library members can borrow laptops and Wi-Fi hotspots for up to three weeks. Other libraries lend musical instruments, from ukuleles to keyboards. These programs are especially popular with students and with families who cannot afford to buy expensive items they will only use occasionally.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the most unusual collections is a 'library of things', where members can borrow tools such as drills, ladders and sewing machines. Organizers say the idea saves money and reduces waste, since many tools are used for only a few minutes in their whole lifetime. Borrowers must watch a short safety video before they can take power tools home.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Libraries have also started lending passes to local attractions. With a library card, families in many cities can borrow a free pass to museums, art galleries or the zoo. In one large city, the passes are so popular that they are usually all reserved within an hour of becoming available each week, and the library has asked attractions to provide more.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is enthusiastic about these changes. Some residents worry that libraries are spending too much on items that break or are never returned, money that could be used to buy more books. Library managers respond that the new items attract people who would not otherwise visit, and that many of these new visitors also start borrowing books.
